planting.note: Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil after the last hard freeze; established clumps shrug off cold, wet winters better than most agave selections.

directions: This selection of Parry's agave forms a tight, nearly globular rosette of broad, blue-gray leaves edged with small reddish teeth and a short terminal spine. It is prized among cold-climate agave growers as one of the hardiest forms of the species, tolerating freezing temperatures and wet winter soils that would rot many other agaves. Plant in gravelly or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; it produces few or no offsets, so it stays a tidy single specimen for years. Water only during extended summer drought and avoid winter irrigation to prevent crown rot.

planting.note: Plant in a sunny, sharply drained spot or container after frost danger passes; this dwarf form is especially well suited to pots.

directions: A dwarf, seed-grown form of Queen Victoria agave, 'Compacta' makes an exceptionally tight, nearly spherical rosette of thick, dark green leaves marked with crisp white edges and veining. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than the typical species, rarely exceeding a foot across, which makes it a favorite for containers, rock gardens, and tight spaces. Grow in gritty, mineral soil in full sun with excellent drainage, and water sparingly, only when the soil has dried out completely. It is extremely slow-growing and monocarpic, so expect it to persist as an ornamental centerpiece for many years before flowering.

planting.note: Plant in full sun to light shade in hot climates, in well-drained soil, after the last frost.

directions: This compact, solitary thread-leaf agave selection forms a symmetrical rosette of dark green leaves decorated with faint white bud-print markings and curling white marginal fibers that peel from the leaf edges. Originally collected along the Mazatlan-Durango highway in Mexico, it is valued for its refined, almost sculptural texture compared to the wild species. Grow in full sun along the coast or light shade in hot inland gardens, in fast-draining, gritty soil, with occasional irrigation in late spring and summer. It is hardy to around 15F and makes an excellent specimen in the garden or in a container.

planting.note: Plant in part sun to light shade in a spot with excellent drainage; unlike most agaves this species prefers some protection from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: A striking sport of the spineless squid agave, 'Stingray' forms an octopus-like rosette of narrow, gracefully arching leaves, each banded with a broad creamy-yellow stripe down the center or margins. The foliage lacks the sharp terminal spines typical of most agave species, making it safer to plant near walkways or in small gardens. It grows slowly and produces only a few offsets, forming a tidy clump over time, and unlike most agaves it survives flowering rather than dying afterward. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil with part-day sun and only occasional water once established.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; give this large hybrid plenty of room to spread.

directions: A large, naturally occurring hybrid agave discovered in San Luis Potosi, Mexico, 'Mr. Ripple' forms a massive rosette of broad, satiny blue-green leaves whose margins undulate dramatically along their length, catching light and shadow in a way few other agaves do. Each heavily armed leaf curves and ripples, giving the whole plant a sculptural, almost liquid presence in the landscape. Among the larger hybrid agaves it is relatively cold-tolerant, so site it in full sun with sharp drainage, and water only during prolonged summer drought. Allow generous space, as mature specimens can spread several feet wide and make a dramatic focal point.
